utterances.text: Do you know what my position was with regard to any unlawful actions and my opposition to any sort of manipulative activities, bribery, corruption, and do you know that I always insisted strictly that all those who were involved with me in the political life should be clean, crystal clean, on that score?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that. I'm familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: For a while, you were present in the buildings where I resided with my family. Were you able to observe me, personally, or my family becoming richer and richer on any score?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: I was there, and I saw nothing that would indicate that you were accumulating any sort of wealth. What I can say is that you were, in that respect, the same, you and your family, from Day 1 until the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How were we? What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: Well, you were as you had always been. You did not gain anything of material value. You did not change in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell Their Honours what sort of attitude I had, as well as my family, towards you, all of the members of the security detail?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: We had a very proper and decent relationship, full of mutual respect and trust.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree with me that I spent a great deal of time in Geneva, Brussels, Lisbon, attending various international conferences, and that I was frequently away from home?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree you were away travelling quite often, especially in the early days of the conflict, in 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that at the time when you started accompanying me on my travels, you were unable to communicate with anyone but the escort detail within the range of five kilometres?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. We had the mobile radio set which -- the range of which was not very far.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you agree that I didn't have anything that would be more sophisticated? They knew that I didn't have a telephone or a radio in my car, and I wasn't able to communicate with anyone outside of the range of three to five kilometres? ^

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree. And if we learned anything over the radio set we had, we would be the ones communicating it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were shown a telegram today which informed the security structures of the imminent passage of the president and other functionaries. On that occasion, they were on their way to Srebrenica. Was this the usual sort of dispatch which was intended to provide information to the military and the police?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. This was just one of the many travels and one of the usual dispatches accompanying it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that a motorcade of some three to five cars was not a daily occurrence, and it was important for the army and the police to know who it carried so that they know how to conduct themselves?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree. At that time, there weren't many vehicles to be had, and fuel was scarce, and it was a rare occurrence, really, to see two cars travelling together in a column.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that there was always the risk of running into either a sabotage group, or a group of stragglers of the enemy army, or combat?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree. Of course, there was always that risk.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you see or hear that we visited the residents of Donji Vakuf at a time when we were actually being showered by shells?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was there, I was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that shells started landing around us at the point when we were heading towards Bronzani Majdan, close to Banja Luka? Mortar shells were landing all around us?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that the police suggested that luxury cars or civilian clothing should not be used, because then it would give an indication of an important delegation coming, which would place at risk both those involved and the residents of the area visited?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Am I right if I say that it was for those reasons only that I would, on occasion, put on a military uniform, and that I did not normally wear one at Pale?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, and this was what the security structure advised you, too, to do, and that's why you wore the military uniform, as you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned presidents of crisis staffs. Do you agree that after the 1st of June, most of the crisis staffs were abolished? And when you said so, did you mean presidents of municipalities and local authorities, who visited the government in order to obtain some sort of assistance?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't familiar with their roles, and I don't know how long the staffs existed. I know that they were presidents of municipalities, presidents of crisis staffs. The purpose of their visits was mainly what you said and to get information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to ask you about the situation at Pale. Do you remember that I was able to rub shoulders, as it were, with the Croats and Muslims who were residents at Pale?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: Well, of course. There were many such opportunities, especially in the early days around the break-out of the conflict in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall also that the mosque and the Catholic Church at Pale remained intact?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that my hairstylist, who had a private salon in the Hotel Panorama building, was a Croat?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: I know the person, but I didn't know her ethnicity, though most probably she was Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, was Pale a dangerous place to be for Croats and Muslims, during the time you were there, or was it quite safe? To be more precise, did you hear of a single incidence of prosecution or any sort of abuse against the Muslims and Croats at Pale? I'm not asking about Renovica.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You described the trip to Srebrenica. Was it a brief journey, and was the return trip on that same day?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was just a short journey, and we returned in the afternoon of the same day. I don't when, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that there was no commander of the Drina Corps or any other official -- or any other officer of the VRS with us?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I remember, there was not a single VRS officer with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that we never visited the municipality either at Bratunac, Vlasenica, Milici, Han Pijesak, Srebrenica? Wherever we went, we never visited any representatives of local authorities?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, we did not visit either the municipalities or local authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that there were no encounters with either the military or civilian authorities during that journey?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that we visited a church which was roofless, it didn't have any doors, there were just the walls standing, frescoes were devastated, and, as you say, there were excrements of various sorts of farm animals?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you also remember that we next attended a prayer service next to a cross deep into the mountain, where a religious ceremony was taking place?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I did say so in response to the Prosecutor's question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I do agree with you, but I'm afraid it's not clear that it was not in Srebrenica, itself. It was deep in the hills?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: Well, I did say that it was a hill close to Srebrenica. I don't know the specifics, but it was pretty distant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that it is part of our tradition that where somebody was killed or perished, initially, where the intention is to make a memorial site of sorts, you would first erect a cross, with the intention of going on to build a memorial site which never ends up built?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you will agree with me that the character of this trip was -- of this visit, that is, was solely religious, and it boiled down to this religious service?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In addition to the church, the destroyed church that we visited, did you have any knowledge at the time of anything else happening in Srebrenica, other than a military operation? Were there any indications of there having happened anything else but a military operation?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: The only knowledge I had was about the military operations, and the groups of stragglers who were fleeing the area, but were still lingering in the general area. And I knew that there was still some fighting going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since there were no meetings taking place indoors, rather, everything was taking place outdoors, did anyone at this particular meeting mention any sort of killings or unlawful actions in Srebrenica? Were there any comments, innuendos, made to that effect?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: I don't recall any such thing happening, any comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we say that you were present during that visit, and that as you returned from it, you didn't have any knowledge of either destruction or killings in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: Well, you can put it that way. We returned without knowing anything about any killings or destruction taking place in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You formed an impression. You were close by. You were treated by the family quite openly. There were no encounters hidden from you. So can you tell us, as a whole, what was my attitude toward crime or unacceptable sort of treatment of either the Serbs or the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: Well, you always condemned any crime, regardless of who it was directed against. You were opposed to that, and you would protest and speak your mind accordingly whenever it happened, and in quite strong language.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ristic, how would you characterise me; as a tolerant, mild, or as a distant person, rigid, strict? Was I the sort of person who had a great deal of tolerance in him and who was open and available to all those who wanted to get in touch with me? Was I easily reachable, was I open to encounters?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: As far as I, myself, am concerned, I have nothing but positive opinion of you. You could be reached easily, and you were quite a tolerant person. When I say that you could be reached easily, you would receive everyone, talk to everyone, and tried to see what you could do to address a matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that many people wanted to take a photograph with me and that it was, indeed, possible for all, and not even you, as the security detail, were able to prevent this from happening?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall this, because we had quite a lot of difficulty with this, in terms of providing security.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were able to see the various secretaries at work, and you were shown a book that they maintained of my appointments. Would you agree that very often I would leave my office late at night, sometimes at 2.00 or 3.00 in the morning, but, at any rate, after 8.00 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. You spent long days at the office. And when you came home, you only had a couple of hours sleep before you returned to the office again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree with me that the secretaries would keep note of who would go into my office, the date, hour, and when they went out of the office, as well as all my telephone contacts?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know that records were kept. I don't know the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is there anything you'd like to say that I haven't asked you about, Mr. Ristic, and something that the Prosecutor has asked you about, is there anything that you would like to state?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: No, there isn't anything I would like to add or state.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Excellencies, my examination is finished. Thank you, Mr. Ristic, for coming here and testifying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, you're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, I do have some re-examination, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: First of all, I want to talk a little about your statement of a few minutes ago, that when you were in Srebrenica on the 4th of August, 1995, that there was no reference at all to any killings of any kind. Was there any reference at all to the Serb soldiers who had died during the Srebrenica operation?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. The impression I gained was that the memorial was in the memory of all the Serbian victims in the area. I think that was mentioned now, be it soldiers or civilians who perished in and around Srebrenica during the war until 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Is it your belief that no Serb soldiers died during the Srebrenica operation?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: I don't think nobody was killed. That's my opinion. I don't have any knowledge of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: At the religious ceremony, was there any acknowledgment of the sacrifice of any Serb soldiers during the Srebrenica operation?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: Definitely not. It was only at a later date when I learned certain things about Srebrenica from the media. I could not believe my ears. During my visit to Srebrenica, there was nothing to make that impression on me. I thought that this was simply some sort of a propaganda campaign.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Going back to the religious ceremony, who provided security for the president at that ceremony?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: The chief of security, who was my superior too.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Were there any military personnel whatsoever present at the religious ceremony?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: No, there weren't. As I said, no military personnel was present at the ceremony. There was no army close to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you know where, exactly, the ceremony was held?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: It was a hill above Srebrenica which could not be reached by car. I do recall us going there on foot, and the slope was quite steep. We went up-hill, and we helped the president climb it. That's why I remember it. But I don't know the exact location. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: How far was the hill from the town of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: I can give you an assumption. Let's say, perhaps, five kilometres. But, at any rate, in the Srebrenica surroundings.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Perhaps we can call up the map that you marked earlier and you could help us identify where that hill was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I request 02227A, please. Could we zoom in on the area around the town of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I can provide you with a hard copy of this map, Mr. Ristic, if that would help you identify where this hill was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And also why don't we zoom in further --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- concentrating on Srebrenica, I think. Much further. I think the circled area appears to be Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: To the right, further, further. To the right. The other way around. No, the other way around, further. You see Srebrenica there, so we zoom in further. Zoom in. Go down, let's go down. No, no, the other way. Yes, go down further. Go down, go down. Yes. We can zoom in once again. Can you mark the place, Mr. Ristic, now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't even begin to guess where we could have been. I really don't know even in which direction it was. There's no way for me even to guess, never mind mark the place. I'm really sorry. Even if I were in Srebrenica, I wouldn't be able to find the place, and I can't find my way around the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'll continue, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You told us earlier that the hill was five kilometres, I think you said, from the town of Srebrenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: Approximately. I assumed that it was that distance, but I don't have the precise information of the name of the hill or how far it was. I just know that it was close by and it was a hill near Srebrenica, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In one of the documents that was shown to you earlier, there is a reference to the presence of enemy groups in this part of Bosnia. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, were you concerned for the president's security as you were escorting him to that hill?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Were you aware that Srebrenica had fallen several months earlier and had fallen under control of the Serb Army? Several weeks earlier; correction.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew that. We also knew that there were some Muslim armed groups who had fled, who were withdrawing towards the Central Bosnia territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Was the army presence around Srebrenica a concern for the security of the president as he attended the religious ceremony at that hill about five kilometres from Srebrenica, by which I mean were the military also concerned about the president's security?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: I really don't know. This was usual for us. We did this throughout the war. We were always in a certain state of stress. There was always that note of tension that an incident can happen at any time, that we were in a state of war, and that we were not safe wherever we went.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Is it your evidence to Their Honours that the security for the president, as he attended that ceremony, consisted only of his personal security detail?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes, his personal security detail and just the regular security that escorted us from the special unit of the MUP. They went with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: There was absolutely no military presence whatsoever as the president went to the religious ceremony and at the religious ceremony; is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this has already been answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sometimes certain questions can be re-asked again, in particular given the answers in a previous set of questions. Yes, please go ahead. This is okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you answer that question, please, Mr. Ristic, or would you like me to repeat it?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: There's no need to repeat it. As far as I know and remember, I didn't see any member of the military, I didn't see any soldiers or officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to call up, please, 03199E. If we could zoom in on that building, please. There's no translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you recognise that building, Mr. Ristic?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: I know this is an Islamic religious facility. I don't know which one, though. All of these buildings are similar, as far as I'm concerned, so I don't know exactly where this one is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, I'll just inform Their Honours and the Defence that this is a combination of three stills from a video taken on the 14th of July, 1995, in Srebrenica town. We'll return to this later in the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you see a building that looked like this in the centre of Srebrenica on the 4th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this was answered as well, that he is squeezing his own witness about things that he didn't see and which he had already answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He wasn't asked specifically whether he remembers having seen a building which is similar to this at the time when he visited Srebrenica. Mr. Ristic, can you answer the question? The question was whether you saw a building that looked like this in the centre of Srebrenica on the 4th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't recall seeing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I can tender this as an exhibit now, Your Honours, on the basis of what the witness has said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On what grounds, I kindly ask?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: On the ground that the witness was in the centre of Srebrenica town and he did not observe this minaret on the 4th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have no information at this moment that this is at the centre of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall I mark it for identification?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When you have some -- can present some foundation for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, we'll be returning to it later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll do that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI P2846, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You wanted to say something, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said -- the witness said that he did not recall seeing it, not that, I did not see it. I do not recall seeing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that has been noted, and that's why we're marking this for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, in one of your answers to Mr. Karadzic's questions, Mr. Ristic, you said that you returned to Pale on the afternoon of the 4th of August, 1995. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: I said that we returned the same day, in the afternoon, yes, in the evening hours. In any case, we did return quickly, considering the type of the trip. We did return the same day. I don't remember exactly at what time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Was it -- keeping in mind that it was the 4th of August, was it daylight when you returned to Pale?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I think it was still day, daylight. I think it was, and that's why I said that we went and returned while it was still day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you follow the same route home; that is to say, from Srebrenica to Bratunac to Milici, along the road that you marked earlier for Their Honours?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, in your answers with Mr. -- your answers to Mr. Karadzic, you said that you did not stop at any point along the route. Did you stop even for a rest break, a meal break, a drink of any kind, even a brief stop?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: I really don't remember any details of that trip. There were many trips. I don't know. I cannot even remember if we stopped anywhere to freshen up. I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Is it therefore possible, yes or no, that you may have stopped in the town of Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: It's possible, but it was probably just a short stop for us to take a little break, Bratunac-Milici. It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to call up now 03199F.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: While that's coming, could you describe the location of the Serb Orthodox Church in the centre of -- in Srebrenica town where you saw evidence that animals had been kept? Was that in the centre of town or where was it?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: It was the first time that I was in Srebrenica, and I just passed through, so I really wasn't aware where the centre of the town was. I assumed that because there were some buildings around, that it was the kind of extended centre where the church was located.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, there will be evidence led later in the trial that this is the same location as the photograph you saw earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: My question to Mr. Ristic is simply this: Do you see that location, Mr. Ristic? Can you recognise that at all?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: No, I don't recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And simply to clarify your evidence on this point, would you -- do you recall at all whether you saw a minaret during your visit to the Serb Orthodox Church and your walk within the town of Srebrenica, or did you not see a minaret during your period in Srebrenica town?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: We didn't walk through Srebrenica. We went by cars, and I didn't see any. I don't remember seeing anything similar to what we're seeing in this photograph, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you at any stage learn of the killing of Muslim men and boys in large numbers in the Srebrenica area?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that at the time. I didn't have any information about it. I knew that military or combat operations were underway, but I didn't have the information. No, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: When did you first hear of that?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I can't really say. I think through the media. It was after -- some time after the date that it happened. A lot of time went by since, and then I received information about it with a dose of reserve.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And can you put a date as to when you first became aware of the killings of Muslim men and boys in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: No, no, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I want to return to the question of radios. Did you -- as a member of the president's personal detail, did you have a personal radio for your work?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did other members of the president's security detail each have their own radio?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes, he had his own radio and his own code.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In your evidence, in response to questions put to you by Mr. Karadzic, you referred to the radio at the Villa Sipad, and you said that that radio -- you agreed with the suggestion that that radio had a radius of about five kilometres. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What was the radius of the personal radio which you carried on your person?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: Well, yeah, it was about the same as that one, but the more powerful radio station had a range of perhaps up to seven kilometres. It was a stationary one in the base with the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Was that a mobile radio? Could you carry it in your hand?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: The one that was at the base was a stationary one. It was installed there and it was located there. The other ones were mobile radio stations, Motorolas.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I want to look now at the radios which were carried in the presidential convoy. And if we could bring up, please, an exhibit. I'll just get the number now. P2784 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you tendering this photo?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That being the case, we'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI P2847, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'm not sure what the timing is, Your Honours. Please feel free to stop me whenever you want.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Could we call up P278 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not clear to me on what basis this photograph is being admitted through this witness. He didn't recognise it, he didn't see it at the time. Simply, I don't see the sense of admitting it through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's just marked for identification, and if later on it turns out that this is to be the centre of Srebrenica, we have the evidence that the witness couldn't recall this site. That's just simply like that. Yes, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could look at P2784, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This concerns questions which were put to you in cross-examination concerning the president's access to communications during convoys. Now, if we look at the next page in English, please, and the final paragraph in your version, Mr. Ristic. I'll read out the relevant portion. Well, really, it relates to the call-signs Beta 1, Beta 11 and Beta 31. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes, but the last one is Beta 31, not 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, are those call-signs, Beta 1, Beta 11 and Beta 31, are they references to radios carried by you and other members of the president's security detail?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes, and these are call-signs for security detail members.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Are these your personal radios of your -- of your group of colleagues?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: How would you make contact with the RS MUP personnel along the convoy route to inform them of the approach of the convoy?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: Well, the dispatch was sent. They were taking these other measures. They were waiting for us and then escorting us. I don't know as for radio links. We didn't have any. We were not in range until we got within -- very close. I mean, it had a range of five kilometres, so when we got very close, then we could communicate with them. Otherwise, the links were used to -- for us to communicate amongst ourselves, among the parties in the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You said one of your duties, I think earlier, was to receive messages coming in for the president. I think you said that in your response to answers to Mr. Karadzic. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: I really -- I don't remember. Could you please repeat it for me?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. If you would give me one moment, please. There was a reference. I'm not able to find it right now. I can return to this after the break, Your Honours. I can move now to another subject or we can take the break now, as Your Honours wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How much longer would you expect?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: It would take no more than about 15 minutes. There are some issues which arose in the cross-examination. I would like to consult with a couple of my colleagues about those prior to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. If it is convenient, then we'll take a break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break for an hour, and we'll resume at 1.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.26 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Ristic, in his questions to you, Mr. Karadzic put to you the fact that you accompanied him on visits to Belgrade. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: How would you travel when you accompanied the president on his visits to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: By car, most of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And when you did not travel by car, how would you travel?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: Well, a few times by helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I want to move to the question of radios. This was something I briefly addressed before the break. At page 46, Mr. Karadzic raised with you the questions of radios within the presidential convoy, and he said, in his question: "Do you agree that I didn't have anything that would be more sophisticated? They knew that I didn't have a telephone or radio in my car, and I wasn't able to communicate with anyone outside the range of five to ten kilometres?" Your answer was: "Yes, I agree, and if we leaned anything over the radio set we had, we would be the ones communicating it to you." Do you remember that question and answer?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What kind of information would you be communicating to the president in those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. The witness said "had that been the case, we would have." He did not put it this way. [In English] "If/would." "If/would."

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's not how it came out in the English interpretation, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that question includes the question whether he had ever conveyed a message to you, so I think the witness can answer the question. Yes, Mr. Ristic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not have an opportunity to convey any kind of information, and I do not recall that anyone else did. But, basically, we would have done that because we were the only ones who had the communications equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'll move on to the trip of the 4th of August, 1995, that we discussed earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, during his cross-examination, Mr. Karadzic put to you a couple of questions and answers, and I'm going to read those out to refresh your memory. He said: "Since there were no meetings taking place indoors, rather, everything was taking place outdoors, did anyone at this particular meeting mention any sort of killings or unlawful actions in Srebrenica? Were there any comments, innuendos, made to that effect?" Your answer was: "I don't recall any such thing happening, any comments." The next question was: "Can we say that you were present during that visit, and that as you returned from it, you didn't have any knowledge of either destruction or killings in Srebrenica? "A. Well, you can put it that way. We returned without knowing anything about any killings or destruction taking place in Srebrenica." Do you remember that exchange?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, on the route the convoy took, which you've marked earlier, the convoy, both to and from Srebrenica, passed through a settlement called Kravica. Do you wish to see the map to confirm that?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: There's no need for a map. I know, roughly, where that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you know of a warehouse at Kravica?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to call up, please, 03199G. This photograph dates from 1996, I believe. It will be tendered later in the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The picture you're seeing, do you recognise that building at the bottom at all, Mr. Ristic?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What is that building?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, can you see the distance between that building and the road?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If Mr. Registrar could push the picture so that the road is visible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you see the distance between the building and the road, Mr. Ristic?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, the Trial Chamber has been made aware - this is adjudicated fact 1075 - that on the evening of the July 13th, 1995, approximately 1.000 Bosnian Muslim men were executed at this location. And Beara and Deronjic and others began organising the burials of those executed. That's Fact 1709. Have you ever heard of those events?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Was there any discussion -- sorry, one other thing. The Trial Chamber has also been made aware of the fact that the men executed were taken there from the meadow at Sandici, which is also on the convoy route. Was there any discussion as you passed Kravica or as you passed Sandici to those events?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: I don't remember, I don't know at all. Kravica, I know it as a location from earlier on, because a crime had been committed against Serb civilians in Kravica in 1992 or 1993; I can't remember exactly. That is how I know that place, Kravica, and that we passed through it. That's why I remember it. I don't remember it by anything else.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I kindly ask the Prosecutor to clarify the word missing at page 23, line 13. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'll make that clarification. One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 23?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Is it page 68, perhaps; interpreter's correction. The sentence: "Was there any," and then there's a missing word, "between there and ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Line 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: My question was this: I was referring to the fact that the Trial Chamber has been made aware of the fact that 1.000 to 1.500 Bosnian Muslim men were captured and detained at Sandici Meadow and then brought to Kravica warehouse, and where they were executed, and their burial was organised by Beara and Deronjic and others. My question was: Was there any discussion within your convoy relating to those events during the trip or after you returned to Pale?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: No. Had there been any, I would have remembered it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Would you repeat your answer, please, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: No, there was no discussion in relation to these killings, because had that happened, that is a big thing, I would have remembered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You worked for Mr. Karadzic or President Karadzic until what year?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: 2000, the year 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you ever hear him express any remorse about events which took place in Srebrenica in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: I don't know what to say to you by way of an answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you answer the question? Did you ever hear him express remorse for the events which took place at Srebrenica in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I have no further questions in redirect. The picture of Kravica warehouse which is on the screen, could I request that that be MFI'd, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see the need to MFI it at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well. Very well, Mr. President. No further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, two brief clarifications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which is what? Tell us first, before putting the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First, Mr. Gaynor implied that the witness had said that I had known about these events and that I did not state my views on them. And the second question is as if the witness had observed Sandici and been aware that we had passed through some Sandici. And then the third has to do with the helicopter that we travelled on. Those are three brief questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well, proceed. Further Cross-examination by Mr. Karadzic:

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ristic, Mr. Gaynor asked you, and you confirmed, that sometimes there was travel to Belgrade by helicopter. Am I right if I say that these were large MI-8 medical helicopters for the evacuation of wounded persons and that we landed by the VMA, the Military Medical Academy in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes, these were helicopters that transported seriously-wounded persons to the Military Academy, the Military Medical Academy in Belgrade. MI-60 -- no, MI-8, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And we used that, we availed ourselves of that opportunity to travel; it wasn't that the helicopters came for us?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we availed ourselves of that opportunity, and also for security reasons, because sometimes roads were cut off, there were offensives around Zvornik, as far as I can remember, and that is why we were -- that is why you used this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Gaynor asked you whether you saw some men in Sandici. Were you actually aware of us passing through some Sandici?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of that, nor do I know to this day where this Sandici is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Third question: He asked you whether I expressed any remorse with regard to what had happened in Srebrenica. Did you ever come to realise that I had actually learned what had really happened in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: My impression was that you did not at all have any responsibility, that you knew something that you should express your remorse over, I mean, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In the environment where I was, was there any conversation to that effect, except for what you mentioned, the media, what had happened in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: No, no. I find all of this foreign, everything regarding Srebrenica, only from the media.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions for you, Mr. Ristic. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we know the -- your date of birth, if you don't mind, or at least your year of birth?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: On the 9th of January, 1972.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you still in the police now?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I ask what you are doing now?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: Now? Now I'm in trade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Earlier on, you said you worked for Mr. Karadzic until the year of 2000. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: Well, 2000, sort of. I don't remember exactly until when.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you remember when he stepped down from the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: No, I don't remember. I can assume when it was. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you served as his security guard, or personal security, after he stepped down from the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA RISTIC
utterances.text: I was an employee of the Ministry of the Interior all the way up until then. That was my duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that concludes your evidence. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: No further questions. I just wanted to say that the translation has been up-loaded off the photographs marked by Mr. Ristic for P2481. But I have no further questions for Mr. Ristic. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And that will be checked and will be sorted out later on. Thank you, Mr. Ristic. That concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Trial Chamber and the Tribunal, as a whole, I'd like to thank you for your coming all the way to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, on behalf of the Defence as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we call the next witness, can I make this observation, Mr. Tieger. I note that while the Prosecution had originally estimated that it would require one and a half hours to examine this witness and present his evidence pursuant to Rule 92 ter, actually, Mr. Ristic ultimately testified entirely viva voce, and Mr. Gaynor only used one hour and fourteen minutes to examine him in his examination-in-chief. So in light of this experience, and given that the use of Rule 92 ter does not always seem to result in a reduction of the in-court time used by the Prosecution, I would, therefore, recommend you to consider, where possible and, in particular, when it would not increase the time for your examination-in-chief, leading witnesses viva voce, as opposed to presenting them pursuant to Rule 92 ter, as in the case of Mr. Ristic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, of course, we'll take the Court's comments on board. May I simply note that the comparison in this case may be a bit misleading for a number of reasons. I've also found myself in that situation, and it can be the result of a variety of factors, including, under the circumstances, jettisoning material that would otherwise be considered useful, the fact that a re-calculation of the amount of time that would have been devoted to a 92 ter, plus some viva voce, wasn't made in light of the decision to go totally viva voce, and the particular witness involved. But, nevertheless, I understand the Court's point, and we will certainly pass it on to every member of the team and consider it accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll excuse myself, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you need a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It will certainly take Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff a few moments to log on. I don't see any reason why we couldn't break for a few minutes so she could do that comfortably, but I leave that to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll break for five minutes, then. --- Break taken at 1.56 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. If you could kindly take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Davidovic. Please be seated, and make yourself comfortable. Good afternoon, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Milorad Davidovic. I was born on the 13th of February, 1951.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Davidovic, you provided a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in 2005, and you also testified here at the Tribunal in the case against Momcilo Krajisnik in 2005 and in the case against Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin in 2010; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In the last few days, did you have an opportunity to review an amalgamated statement consolidating relevant parts from your previous statement and testimonies?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would ask that Exhibit 65 ter 90250 be brought up on the screen, and we need the first page in both languages, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, Mr. Davidovic, as it is coming up, it is a statement dated 22nd June 2011. Is this the amalgamated statement that you reviewed and later on signed?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In relation to paragraph 40 in the amalgamated statement, where you describe a visit to Pale and the transport of weapons and equipment, do you wish to clarify a point related to the transport of equipment and weapons?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if anything needs clarifying on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: On this first occasion that you went to Pale, did you bring weapons with you and equipment?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: The first time I went there, I brought along some equipment, several uniforms, and short-barrelled weapons. The second time I went there, we went by helicopter, and we brought along a larger amount of equipment and weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, the witness has the amalgamated statement in front of him. I don't know whether you mind that. Otherwise, we would have to always pull up that particular paragraph here in electronic form. It would be much quicker to simply refer him to the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in relation to paragraph 77 in the amalgamated statement, you refer to the elite units in the RS MUP, and you also mention Dusko Malovic and their degree of skills and training. Do you wish to clarify to which elite units you are referring and what their skills were at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I said that those units were called special units and that they did undergo some training, which meant that they were professionally trained to accomplish their mission, whatever the circumstances. I did not gain the impression that it was an elite unit which was fully equipped and one which could carry out everything that they were told to do. They were volunteers, and from what I know, Dusko Malovic was an active-duty serviceman who gathered these men at Sokolac, trained them, and that's how they created conditions for work.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the exception of these two clarifications and additions, just one additional point.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you affirm that the amalgamated statement of 22nd June 2011 accurately reflects the evidence you provided to the Office of the Prosecutor and the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, would you provide that same evidence to the Court if questioned on the same matters here today?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It wouldn't be the same, in terms of every word, but I'm sure that I would repeat 99 per cent of what I said earlier on without any problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender this statement for admission under Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I would like to be heard about this, but I think it would be more prudent to be heard outside the presence of the witness. Would you mind to excuse the witness so that I could be heard more fully?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise for your inconvenience, Mr. Davidovic. There are certain matters to discuss in your absence. If you could please excuse yourself for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was wondering whether or not you would consider, in part, in light of what your comment was at the end of the last witness, to whether this witness could be heard viva voce, rather than by admission of his amalgamated statement under 92 ter. In addition to the time element, which the Prosecution has reserved three hours for the direct examination of this witness, so it's possible that there may not be much of a time savings, there are some other aspects of this witness's testimony that would make, in our submission, it more appropriate for viva voce testimony. First, it's going to be very contentious, and you could see from the allegations that the witness makes against Dr. Karadzic, himself, that there are many things in his statement that we don't accept and, in fact, find offensive. And, secondly, the amalgamated statement contains matters that we think are irrelevant and prejudicial, concerning allegations of corruption, gambling, extortion of -- or proceeds of extortion going to Dr. Karadzic, so we think there are things in the amalgamated statement that ought not to be admitted into evidence under any circumstances. For all of those reasons, we would ask that the Chamber consider hearing this witness viva voce, rather than under 92 ter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before I hear from the Prosecution, I note that submission is too much belated. I could not but say that. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And, Your Honours, I have spent two days now going, with the witness, through the amalgamated statement, and I can actually say using the amalgamated statement would be an enormous time saving because the witness has so many additional -- additional little details that he would want to tell the Court, which we wouldn't really need, but he's a person who is very meticulous and wants to tell the details. Definitely, if we would have to have his evidence live, it would take definitely two days, or even more than that. So the time saving in this situation is definitely a point, an important point. The testimonies that he gave in the past took days and days, and I think it's not a good -- it's not a good example to do this. The witness, of course, gives a lot of information in relation to the character of Mr. Karadzic and his war profiteering, as I may call it that, and I think it is relevant to this case. And, definitely, I assume that he will spend a lot of time in cross-examination dealing with these claims that the witness makes in his amalgamated statement, and he has the right to do so, and I expect him to do so. And just one additional point. I, myself, will not address these kind of matters any further in my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, the Chamber does not see the need to convert the nature of this witness into a viva voce witness. The fact that the content of the witness's evidence may be contentious does not necessarily warrant that witness to be heard live, and in addition to the fact you raised the issue too belatedly. We don't see any prejudice by admitting his statement pursuant to Rule 92 ter, in particular given his answer to the question by Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. So we deny your motion. Let's bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just also indicate that if you look at the associated exhibits - this is on a different topic - we have an objection to some of them, and I just thought I should let the Prosecution know. There's about 14 statements of third parties that are contained in the associated exhibits, and we don't think that it's appropriate to admit those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll deal with them when we come to that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My apologies again for you, Mr. Davidovic. We'll continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender this 92 ter statement now into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted as the next Prosecution evidence. We'll give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the statement of the Witness Davidovic under 65 ter 90250 shall be assigned Exhibit P2848. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your leave, I would like to read a brief summary of the witness's evidence. Mr. Milorad Davidovic, a police officer by profession, served in various positions within the Republican Police in Bosnia and Herzegovina before the war, including the Police Station in Bijeljina. In the second half of 1991, he moved to the Federal Secretariat of Internal Affairs in Belgrade (the Federal SUP). And in his capacity as a member of the Federal SUP, he executed several assignments in Bosnia and Herzegovina during the period relevant to the indictment. Mr. Davidovic observed the transformation of the Bosnia and Herzegovina police structure and the emergence of the Bosnian Serb Ministry of Interior (the RS MUP), and its police formations and their co-ordination and co-operation with the Bosnian Serb civilian and military authorities, as well as police and paramilitary forces from Serbia. The witness was involved in and familiar with the co-ordination and co-operation between the Bosnian Serb leadership, including the accused, and the Belgrade authorities, including officials from the Federal SUP and officials from Serbia. Mr. Davidovic, while on duty in the Federal Commission visiting Bosnia and Herzegovina, noticed the arming of the local population in Bosnia in late 1991 and early 1992, and the build up of the reserve police forces. He, himself, was involved in the transfer of weapons and equipment from the Federal SUP to the RS MUP with the assistance of the Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA. Mr. Davidovic was instructed by the Federal SUP to transfer with a group of police officers to Bosnia and Herzegovina in spring of 1992 to establish -- to assist in the establishment of the RS MUP; in particular, the establishment and training of a special-purposes unit. During this time, the witness observed the presence of paramilitary forces in Sarajevo in 1992 and the criminal activities of such troops as well as those of Bosnian Serb forces. At a meeting with Ratko Mladic and the accused at Lukavica Barracks, he complained about the looting by Serb troops. The witness, in his official capacity as well as a citizen of Bijeljina, directly observed a policy of forcible removal of non-Serbs and crimes committed against them in several areas in Bosnia-Herzegovina, including Bijeljina, Brcko and Zvornik. He, in particular, realised that the Serbian Democratic Party designed and executed a policy of the systematic removal of non-Serbs from Bijeljina from May 1992 until and including 1995. Non-Serb residents were dismissed from their jobs, subjected to various forms of persecution, including arbitrary arrests, detention and murder. Organised looting was conducted by local Serbs, including policemen, as well as paramilitary and volunteer forces from Serbia that were allowed to commit crimes against non-Serbs with impunity. The witness became aware that the accused and other Bosnian Serb leaders regularly visited Bijeljina on their way to and from Belgrade and were closely associated with Serb officials in Bijeljina and financially benefitted from the money and valuables obtained from the non-Serbs. Mr. Davidovic, in conversations with Mico Stanisic, the accused, as well as others, realised that the accused and other members of the Bosnian Serb leadership knew about the presence of paramilitaries in Bijeljina and Zvornik. He took part in a meeting in Belgrade in which the accused and Arkan participated and activities were planned. He also observed the presence of Arkan's men in the Lukavica Barracks when the witness had the meeting with Mladic and the accused. Mr. Davidovic and a group of policemen from the Federal SUP came to Bijeljina in the summer of 1992 and took part in a joint action by the military and the police in Bijeljina, Brcko and Zvornik to arrest members of the paramilitary formations who at that time committed crimes against the Serb population as well, including against officials from Pale. The witness's activities to establish law and order, and his insistence to protect all citizens, including non-Serbs, led to a deterioration of his relations with the local Crisis Staff in Bijeljina. The Bijeljina Municipal Assembly undertook efforts to have the witness expelled from the municipality for arresting too many Serbs and for general anti-Serb behaviour. Although many members of the paramilitary formations were arrested, the witness noticed that the persecution of non-Serbs continued in Bijeljina. During his efforts in Brcko, Mr. Davidovic visited the Luka Camp detention facility in Brcko. At that time, the camp held about 70 Muslims, including children. The witness, while participating in the arrest of members of the Yellow Wasps in Zvornik because of looting, robbery and theft, obtained information about various other crimes, including murders, which they had committed there. In the course of his duties in the Federal SUP, Mr. Davidovic travelled to an Assembly session in Pale in 1993 in which the Vance-Owen Peace Plan was rejected by the Bosnian Serbs despite the fact that Slobodan Milosevic and the Greek prime minister attended this session and were in favour of the plan, and expressed that. Your Honour, that completes the summary, and I have now to ask further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, you described your career in the police from 1974 onwards, and you also mentioned that you became a chief inspector in the Federal SUP. Is this a high-ranking position? And if so, can you tell us where it is positioned within the hierarchy of the Federal SUP?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Can I just make one correction, please? You said that I was transferred to the Federal SUP. Let me tell you that I wasn't transferred. I went to the Federal SUP of my own will, upon my own request. I wasn't transferred by an organ, republican or otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Thank you, Mr. Davidovic. But can you answer my question, where your position as chief inspector is situated in regard of hierarchy?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: When I moved to the Federal SUP, I was assigned to the post of the chief inspector of the police for the former Yugoslavia. Later on, I became deputy commander of the Federal Brigade to the post of the chief inspector, so I was among the 10 top-most officials and my number was number 5, which also denotes the ranking in the leadership structure.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when you were in Bosnia and Herzegovina or when you were communicating with others, on which level would you do this? On which level were your partners, your counterparts?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: It was the minister of the interior of Republika Srpska and his deputy, Cedo Kljajic. In other words, Mico Stanisic and Cedo Kljajic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: As far as you communicated with military, on what level would that be?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Solely through the corps commander and the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In your statement, you describe the joint commission you were part of in September 1991 and how you -- how you investigated and checked the status of the reserve police. In this context, did you also visit the SRB -- the police station in Pale? And if so, what was the situation there in relation to reserve police and arming?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: We visited several centres of the Security Service at the time. Within individual centres, we went to see some of the local SUPs in several locations. When we were checking the work of the Sarajevo centre, we were told to tour several stations. One was Station Centar, then Station Pale, and Kiseljak, I believe. We went about our work, looking through the records, et cetera, and we established that there was a sharp increase in the head count of the reserve force. And depending on the ethnic make-up of a given location, that would be reflected in the make-up of the reserve force. And when we got to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the location.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] ... we realised that there was a major increase in the reserve force. We weren't given proper records, but we realised -- well, we realised, actually, that there was a fluctuation of personnel, though not a major increase. And when we went to the various intersections around Pale, we realised that the check-points that were around the perimeter of Pale were manned mostly by individuals of Serb ethnicity and by those who had joined the MUP only recently through the reserve force. However, there would always be one or two active policemen among the reserve policemen who had been there from before, and this is something that we noted down in our report that we submitted to both the republic and federal SUPs.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't catch the name of the location that you went in Pale. Do you recall which other location you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I was talking about other locations where I was to previously, and then I discussed our visit to Pale and the resulting report that we sent to the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Federal SUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You, yourself, referred in your statement to the fact that in 1990, the Bosnia-Herzegovina reserve police had a strength of about 60.000 to 70.000. What was the increase in 1991/1992 when you checked on this data?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was treble the amount -- the number of personnel that there used to be, three or four times -- three- or four-fold was the increase in most of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You described your tasking and activities in Vraca in the spring of 1992, and you have already provided a lot of details and referred to several intercepted conversations. However, I would like to address one more intercepted conversation with you in this context.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And I would like to have Exhibit 65 ter 30701 brought up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as it is coming up: It is a transcript of an intercepted conversation, dated 21st of April, 1992, between you and Mr. Goran Saric. Mr. Davidovic, do you remember this conversation with --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Mr. Saric is who?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I know Mr. Saric from before the conversation that we had. Mr. Saric completed the Secondary School for the Police Force and then graduated from the Police Academy.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, we wouldn't need all the details. He was a policeman, then?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was an active policeman. He was assistant to the commander of the Novi Grad Police Station.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have page 4 in the English, the top part, and page 2 in the Serbian, the bottom part, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Mr. Saric is telling you that Bijeljina and Zvornik, as well as Krajina, is solved, and that it is known who owns that. What does he refer to here?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is calling for speculation. If this isn't something that is noted down in the conversation, how can the witness know what was meant 20 years later?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, your objection is overruled, Mr. Karadzic. The witness can answer as far as he can remember. Yes, Mr. Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the conversation I had with Goran, I asked him to come and see us at the school in Vraca. His response was that he didn't know what to do because the situation was quite serious in Sarajevo. He said that in Zvornik, in Bijeljina, that the situation was more or less resolved, and I think he meant that it was safe, that the Serbs had taken over power, and that this was no longer the problem. The problem was the town of Sarajevo and how it was going to be resolved, and that's what he means here.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And can we please have the bottom part of page 4 in the English, and in the Serbian, page 3, the lower part.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, you are referring here to Wednesday or Thursday, the 6th or the 7th, as your date of arrival in Pale. Taking into account this is April that you are talking, when would that -- what would that be -- what kind of date would that be?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Precisely those days, yes, those dates.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I request this exhibit to be admitted into evidence because the witness is one of the speakers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be done. We will admit it as Exhibit P2849.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, in your statement, you refer to the school, the Vraca school in which you were situated, and you also mentioned the communications that you had there, the means of communications. Did they function all the time while you were there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They had full communication with Belgrade and with the other organs. I contacted Bijeljina, so I was in contact with them. At that point in time, everything was functioning.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in this context, do you know whether the RS MUP had communications with the CSBs and the SJBs?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think that on the whole, there was always communication, with some small interruptions vis-a-vis certain organs, but very often the communication would be re-established in some other way. So there were communications. If there were -- if the telephone lines were down, then there would be courier communication. So it wasn't that no communication whatsoever could not take place over a longer period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would ask that Exhibit 65 ter 08153 be brought up on the screen, please. And as it is coming up: It is a fax of the chief of the CSB Bijeljina to the RS MUP and, as it says here, to the minister, on the 29th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Jesuric is referring here to his visit to the Zvornik SJB. According to police practice, would CSB chiefs make regular contacts with the SJBs in their field, in their area?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: There were faxes, and beforehand there were teleprinters there, so they stayed there. But most of the communication was by fax, and telephones, and the special communications that the Republican SUP has. This is special communication only between two MUPs; that is to say that there are no other lines that can interfere with that communication.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how frequently would the CSB communicate with the SJBs in their area?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they needed to have daily communication. When the centre covers certain local organs, it has daily communication with them. They ask for information, they communicate and so on. This is customary practice on a daily basis. Sometimes even several times a day, the centre would communicate with the local organ.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And would the police chiefs in the SJBs [sic], as Mr. Jesuric is doing here, inform the minister about their contacts and occurrences?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Precisely, that is their function. And this document that you showed, in which Predrag Jesuric, the chief of the CSB from Bijeljina, is informing the minister about the situation in Zvornik, I would just like to refer to the date when this brief dispatch is being sent.
