And it says that the situation is normal and that there are no serious disruptions in public law and order. And in that period of time, there were crimes being committed, there was looting, and the Yellow Wasps were fully functional. So I think that this information is not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, in your question, did you refer to police chiefs in the SJBs, as Mr. Jesuric?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: CSBs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It should read "CSBs"?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: CSBs, yes. I would like to -- Your Honour, I request the admission of this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, this will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 8153 shall be assigned Exhibit P2850. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can I have another document now pulled up, and that is 65 ter 08278. And it is a very similar document, as we can see here. Mr. Jesuric is now -- is also writing again to the ministry, minister and deputy minister, and it's from the 24th of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Just one question in relation to this, Mr. Davidovic. Can you tell us how frequent such correspondence between the CSBs and the minister would be? What would be the regular practice?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: As a rule, the chief of the CSB has to have daily communication with the minister. When problems crop up in the meantime, then he may communicate several times a day. There are some periods of time when he would not communicate with the minister over two days if nothing special had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Can this document also be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 8278 shall be assigned Exhibit P2851. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, you have mentioned your assignments in Sarajevo, and we do not need to go into this detail. But you refer, in paragraph 50 - but you don't need to look at it right now - that you also, at some point in time, had to defend the front-line near the Jewish cemetery. Only one question to that. Which other Serb formations were in that area?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Members of the army were there and of the active police from Sokolac, who had also come to that area, and among them there were members of the station from Sarajevo who were also sent to that line, that defence line at the Jewish cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you also -- were there also any paramilitary forces at the Jewish cemetery, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the beginning, no. In the beginning, it was more or less volunteers who had come and who were led by Slavko Aleksic. They were volunteers, primarily locals from the surrounding area or Sarajevo. They were volunteers, and they were under the command of the army and they were not paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, you also describe, in relation to your front -- your being on the front-lines you describe in paragraph 52, you describe looting and disorder that you observed, and you referred to people crying and being upset. What people were targeted when you observed this happening?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the Jewish cemetery, between the lines, and at the command where we were, there were residential buildings where people lived, and every day this is what would happen: In apartments where Muslims lived, or where they were living then, ethnic Serbs would move in or barge into those apartments and take things out of them, including technical equipment and whatever was valuable in those apartments. These were active-duty and reserve personnel and locals who were trying to resolve status-related issues in that way; to get into someone else's apartment, to thereby have a place to live, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Davidovic, in paragraph 54 and 55 of your statement, you refer to a talk that you had with Karadzic and Mladic in the Lukavica Barracks, and about how you told them about the looting and that that needed to be stopped. You mentioned that while this talk took place, some Arkan's men arrived, and that Karadzic and Mladic then spoke about it. Can you tell us what, actually, Mladic and Karadzic said in relation to Arkan's men coming there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: When I was at this meeting between myself and Ratko Mladic, it was not expected, but Mr. Karadzic entered the room unannounced. Before he had entered, I had started talking to General Mladic and telling him about this looting, about beating people, and so on, and I told him about some of these moving scenes that I had seen, where people were crying and despairing over such situations. When Mr. Karadzic entered, five or ten minutes later someone said that part of Arkan's unit had arrived. Some young men had come. I remember this very well, because we went out to see. And in front of the command where Ratko Mladic was, a few vehicles stopped, and among them there was a Golf that had its roof cut off. And these young men introduced themselves as members of Arkan's unit who had come to help in the liberation of Sarajevo. Then we went into the office, and the conversation continued on that topic. General Mladic was very angry when he saw these people, because he was totally against the paramilitaries coming, particularly Arkan's unit, and he said, Who sent them, how come they were there? And then in response to that, Mr. Karadzic said, It's all right, we asked them to come. They should help with the liberation of Sarajevo. And, If they can do it, let them do it. Let them take whatever they can take.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to have -- no, I think it takes too much time.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In your statement, you also mentioned an encounter with the paramilitaries in various places, and you, in particular, spoke about a certain Carli with the Red Berets in Sarajevo, and you also mentioned Zika Crnogorac. And in this context, you, in fact, mentioned - and that is paragraph 103 - that you saw a video with Zika Crnogorac, that you saw. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: When I talked about coming to Sarajevo, I didn't say that Arkan was in Sarajevo. I said that there was a person there who was the commander of that unit that had come, and they called him Carli. I never learned his name. That was a unit that had come, equipped by the MUP of Serbia. Carli is what he was called. However, Arkan was not in that area. He was in the area of Zvornik, Bijeljina, elsewhere, whereas Zika Crnogorac - sorry for interrupting - was not there. Zika Crnogorac was in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, but we come to this in more detail. I actually want to stick with Zika Crnogorac only very briefly, and for this I would like to have the video 65 ter 45235 being played. And we only want to see certain parts of it. Before we start doing this: Mr. Davidovic, have you seen a video depicting an award ceremony of the unit of special operations in Kula while you prepared for the testimony? Did you review this video in parts?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I did view that footage, parts of it, although I have to say that I had had it earlier on. I still have it to this day, and I know it. I've known it from before, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have the part 00:22 until 00:1:10 being played.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And if you just would tell us whom you see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is Mr. Jovica Stanisic, and on the right is Legija. He is reporting to him in Kula. Also, Jovica Stanisic. This is Mr. Kertes, Vucetic. This is Zika Crnogorac at the left.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, that is sufficient. But I'm a bit surprised. I thought we have a running transcript, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My information is we do have the transcript, but it's impossible to present it together with the video.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What would be best would be, actually, if the translation booth would have the two transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So shall we do it next week?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Oh, yeah. Yes, we can do that, definitely. I thought it would be here underneath. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. I note the time, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. It's time to rise for the week. This week we have been very efficient and productive, so much so that we have been hearing seven witnesses, starting from Ms. Hanson. We'll rise, and we'll resume 9.00 on Tuesday next week. Please do have a nice weekend, Mr. Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, you usually remind the witness not to talk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I was about to.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And in the meantime during the break, you're not supposed to discuss with anybody else about your testimony. Do you understand that, Mr. Davidovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.
